glossary.Malaise: A general feeling of being unwell, tired and uncomfortable.
glossary.URTI: Upper respiratory tract infection: a cold-like infection of the nose, throat or sinuses.
glossary.Viraemic: Having virus circulating in the blood; usually the most infectious phase.
glossary.Fifth disease: Another name for erythema infectiosum (slapped cheek), caused by parvovirus B19.
glossary.Lacy: A net-like, reticular pattern of rash, as seen on the limbs after slapped cheek.
glossary.Prodrome: Early non-specific symptoms that come before the main signs of a disease.
glossary.Sandpaper rash: A fine, rough-feeling red rash typical of scarlet fever.
glossary.Strep. pyogenes: Streptococcus pyogenes (group A strep), the bacterium behind scarlet fever and tonsillitis.
glossary.Group A strep: Streptococcus pyogenes; causes scarlet fever, tonsillitis and severe invasive infections.
glossary.Vesicles: Small fluid-filled blisters under 5 mm across.
glossary.Pustules: Small raised spots filled with pus.
glossary.Erythematous halo: A ring of red, inflamed skin around a spot or blister.
glossary.Well-demarcated: Having a sharp, clear edge between affected and normal skin.
glossary.Chickenpox: Primary infection with varicella zoster virus, giving an itchy vesicular rash.
glossary.VZV: Varicella zoster virus, the herpesvirus that causes chickenpox and shingles.
glossary.Encephalitis: Inflammation of the brain tissue itself, usually from infection, causing confusion, fits or reduced consciousness.
glossary.Superinfection: A second infection on top of an existing one, such as bacteria in chickenpox spots.
glossary.Necrotising fasciitis: A rapidly spreading, life-threatening bacterial infection that destroys skin, fat and the fascia around muscle.
glossary.Haemolytic: To do with the breakdown of red blood cells.
glossary.Haemolytic anaemias: Anaemias caused by red cells being destroyed faster than normal, e.g. sickle cell disease.
glossary.Bone marrow: Soft tissue inside bones where blood cells are made.
glossary.Antihistamines: Drugs that block histamine to ease itch and allergy symptoms.
glossary.Hypersensitivity: An exaggerated immune reaction that harms the body's own tissues.
glossary.Antigens: Molecules, such as viral proteins, that the immune system recognises and reacts to.
glossary.Exotoxin: A toxin secreted by bacteria into the surroundings.
glossary.Immune suppression: Weakening of the immune system, here a short-lived effect of measles infection.
glossary.Placenta: The organ linking mother and fetus that passes oxygen and nutrients; some viruses can cross it.
glossary.First trimester: The first 12 weeks of pregnancy, when organs form.
glossary.Self-limiting: Gets better on its own without treatment.
glossary.Symptomatic: Treatment aimed at easing symptoms rather than curing the cause.
glossary.Supportive: Care that keeps the patient comfortable and safe while the illness runs its course.
glossary.Secondary bacterial infection: A bacterial infection that takes hold on top of a viral illness.
glossary.Pneumonia: Infection of the lung tissue causing consolidation, cough, fever and breathlessness.
glossary.Erythrovirus: An older name for the genus containing parvovirus B19.
glossary.NSAIDs: Non-steroidal anti-inflammatory drugs, such as ibuprofen; avoided in chickenpox.
glossary.Epithelium: The layer of cells lining skin and mucous membranes.
glossary.Mucosal: To do with the moist lining of the mouth, gut or airways.
glossary.Viral PCR: A test that detects viral genetic material to identify the exact virus.
glossary.School exclusion: Keeping an infectious child off school until they are no longer a risk to others.
glossary.Torso: The trunk of the body: chest, abdomen and back.
